body.text: Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has confirmed changes to the backpacker visa rules.
After pushback from regional Australia, the government has delayed a proposed ballot system for backpackers seeking second and third-year visas until early next year.
None of those changes would affect British backpackers who remain exempt from regional work rules.

Shoebridge says Labor is about to hand down an 'austerity budget'
Greens leader David Shoebridge says the government's upcoming mid-year fiscal and economic outlook will be an "austerity budget".
In a speech this morning, Treasurer Jim Chalmers flagged spending cuts in the budget update due to be handed down in December.
"It will cut enough, but not too much," he told the ASIC Annual Forum. "We take seriously and embrace our responsibilities in the fight against inflation."
The federal government is under pressure to reduce Commonwealth spending as the inflation rate and interest rates rise.
"The treasurer has come out and belled Labor's cat today on an austerity budget that is staring down Australia's Christmas and Australians' New Year," Shoebridge says.
"We've got alternatives to what Labor could do if they're trying to get the budget sorted. Take away the $16.3 billion in fossil fuel subsidies they give to corporate Australia."
Taylor pans EU deal as a 'climate agreement not a free trade deal'
Back to Townsville, where Angus Taylor has repeated his criticism of the Australia-EU free trade agreement.
The Coalition is opposed to the deal, which was finalised by the government in March, due to concerns it binds Australia to climate targets.
The opposition leader says he's a believer of free trade but as it stands the deal is a "climate agreement, not a free trade agreement".
"We will not support making the Paris Agreement binding," Taylor says.

"The New Zealanders have supported it and they've not got complaints running through the EU and through the commission. Because of that we are dead against it. It's the wrong thing to do at this time."
Liberal senator Andrew MacLachlan told ABC Radio National Breakfast this morning that he's willing to cross the floor to vote for the bill.
Coalition tries and fails to suspend standing orders to discuss trusts, CGT
The Coalition has just moved to suspend standing orders in the Senate to discuss Labor's changes to discretionary trusts and capital gains tax.
The motion says the federal government's tax changes, which are before parliament, will impose further financial pressure on Australian families.
It condemns the federal government "for pursuing further tax increases" during a cost-of-living crisis.
Opposition Leader in the Senate Michaelia Cash has told the Senate businesses could face $1.73 billion in further taxation.
"If the Labor Party does proceed with the Australian Greens with putting this toxic tax through, businesses have been pretty clear, they will have to close," Cash said.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher accused Cash of "hyperbole" and says the Coalition is using a Senate standing order to make a political argument.
"We understand that the opposition oppose the tax reform that we have been pursuing," Gallagher said.
The Coalition's motion has been unsuccessful, though. Labor has teamed up with the Greens to pass a closure motion and shut it down.
Canavan labels 'climate talk fest' a 'joke'
Nationals leader Matt Canavan has been asked about criticism of the Coalition from his colleague, Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan.

McLachlan told ABC Radio National Breakfast this morning that his own side was "petty" when it made criticisms about the cost of running a coffee cart at the UN climate change conference COP31 in Türkiye, rather than focusing on climate policy.
"We've got a free and open party room … I've always welcomed that," Canavan says, adding he gets on well with McLachlan.

"I think this climate talk fest in Turkey has been a complete joke, and it's been a joke to the prime minister and to the energy minister as well, they've been seemingly too busy joking rather than doing real work for the Australian public."
That's a reference to when the pair were caught out talking about phone radiation and "dicks" on a hot mic at the summit.
Canavan added that the AI race was an energy race and that Australia risked being left behind when it came to building data centres, compared to nations like China.
"This is a race, this goes to our security, not just our convenience," he said.
Greens won't support parliamentary inquiry on CGT changes ... yet
The Greens won't back a Coalition motion to send Labor's capital gains tax changes to a parliamentary inquiry today, as the party commits to "keeping options open".

Labor's CGT changes would see the existing 50 per cent discount scrapped and replaced with a discount based on inflation and the introduction of a minimum 30 per cent tax on gains from July next year.
Greens treasury spokesman Nick McKim has described independent MP Allegra Spender's proposal of a 40 per cent CGT discount on productive assets as "interesting".
The party won't say whether it supports the proposal, but is flirting with the idea it could be explored further in a parliamentary inquiry.
The Greens are clearly in no mood to help Labor pass its budget reforms through parliament before Christmas, arguing "we're not here to facilitate the government's political aims".

On another matter — the taxation of discretionary trusts — the Greens are pushing Labor hard to abandon a carve-out for tax-free trust payments to private schools, arguing there is "no reason those trusts should get an exemption".
"Labor should go back to the budget night position they had before capitulating to the private school lobby," a Greens spokesperson said.
Taylor 'dead against' backpacker ballot scheme
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor is also taking aim at the government's backpacker backdown.
"They've created a complete mess with this raffle, this ballot. They've said they're going to delay it ... they should just axe it," he says.
The government announced it will lift the regional work requirement for backpackers from three months to four, starting from next March.
It's also proposed changes to its cap on third-year visas, up from 5,000 to 25,000.
Taylor says he's "dead against" the ballot system and would "absolutely" repeal it if the Coalition were elected.
Nationals reject caps on regional backpacker numbers
Nationals leader Matt Canavan says the government's latest backdown over backpacker visas is a "complete and utter disaster".
"The government's migration policy, announced just months ago, has not even made it through to Christmas," he said.

Those changes, which introduced a ballot system and slashed third-year Working Holiday Maker visas to 5,000, "went down like a lead balloon" in regional areas that rely on backpackers for seasonal fruit-picking and to fill workforce shortages.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced changes to those changes today, saying from March next year third-year places would be lifted to 25,000 and second-year visa holders must complete four months of regional work, compared to three months currently.
"This government backdown — another backflip from this government — was inevitable, but the damage has been done to confidence in this sector," Canavan said.

When asked if the four-month change would benefit regional employers, Canavan said he would wait to see what business and farmers had to say, and wanted to see more detail about how the new system would work.
"The fact remains that caps remain in place; we don't see a need for such caps."
Key Event
Major drop in backpacker visa approvals this financial year
The number of backpackers getting visas to Australia has fallen dramatically since July, after the home affairs minister directed his department to go-slow, or pause, visa processing.
This was a temporary fix designed to put the brakes on international arrivals before the broader migration overhaul was unveiled.

Since July, 44,469 visas have been approved, which means a total of 177,876 backpackers would be granted entry to Australia this financial year if the government maintained its current rate of processing.
For context, last financial year a record 323,077 backpacker visas were granted in Australia.
Of those, 77,053 were from the UK, a cohort that is given special treatment under a free trade agreement signed in 2023.
But it's now the fastest growing group and the prime minister is negotiating directly with his British counterpart to curb numbers.
The government's processing go-slow is having an impact; only 9,700 UK backpackers have been granted visas since July, which is a huge drop.
Butler says states can go their own way on puberty blockers
Health Minister Mark Butler says he respects the right of Queensland and the Northern Territory to reject new national advice on the use of puberty blockers.
Puberty blockers are injections that pause aspects of physical development by supressing sex hormones, and they've increasingly become the subject of fierce debate here and abroad.

The National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC) interim advice yesterday recommended puberty blockers remain a clinical option for certain trans and gender diverse children, despite low-certainty evidence about their benefits and harms.

Both Queensland and the Northern Territory have banned or restricted the use of the medication in the public system for trans and gender diverse children, and yesterday dismissed the NHMRC advice saying they'd maintain their existing policies.
Butler says his job was to provide the guidelines, and it's up to each state and territory to decide whether to implement them.

"Rather than have this very highly charged public debate driven and settled by opinion writers in our newspapers, I thought it was important that families and the community have the confidence that clinicians are using the most up-to-date, highest quality clinical guidelines," he said."Every state government will make their own decision about how they deliver services."

"Rather than have this very highly charged public debate driven and settled by opinion writers in our newspapers, I thought it was important that families and the community have the confidence that clinicians are using the most up-to-date, highest quality clinical guidelines," he said.
"Every state government will make their own decision about how they deliver services."
ATO super letters to business 'paused', Chalmers says
Controversial letters to businesses from the ATO about "discrepancies" in their super payments have been paused, Jim Chalmers says.
The letters were reported in the Financial Review, which likened them to Robodebt because they were sent out automatically, and the issue was taken up by shadow treasurer Tim Wilson.

In a statement yesterday, the ATO said the letters were not like Robodebt and were not debt notices at all. Rather, they were notifying businesses of possible discrepancies between the super their employees were reporting, and what their payroll suggested about what should be paid.
The ATO described super underpayment as a "serious problem".

Chalmers says it's a matter for the ATO, but adds that the government has reached out to remind them they should be "respectful" in their communications with business and that the letters are "part of that" obligation. He says he understands the ATO has now paused the letters and is reviewing them.
Burke credits UK backpacker go-slow for lift in third-year ballot cap
A go-slow on the processing of backpackers visas has allowed for the government to make tweaks to its broader proposed changes to the working holiday maker scheme.
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke says because of that the government will still be able to meet its migration targets.
Under a Morrison-era free trade deal, UK backpackers are not required to undertake regional work. Burke calls this "not a good outcome" for Australia.
"We've got constructive conversations that are continuing with the United Kingdom and I'm optimistic that we're going to get a much better deal than was previously negotiated," he says.
The minister says conversations are going "very well" but he doesn't want to pre-empt any decisions.

"The United Kingdom have a good understanding of the issues that we need to resolve. So I'm not going to put a timeline on it, but I will say I'm very optimistic about how those conversations have been going," he says.
Burke says it's the slower processing of the UK backpackers visas that allowed him to increase the third-year ballot up a proposed 5,000 cap to 25,000.
Key Event
Backpackers to be required to work in the regions for longer to stay
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has just stepped up in Cairns, where he confirms a change to the backpacker visa rules.
From March, the number of days working holiday makers will have to complete in the regions to be eligible for a second year will increase from 88 days to 120 days.
The cap on the number of third-year visas under the proposed ballot system will rise from 5,000 to 25,000.
"This creates a very significant shift, but also means for the people who are wanting to qualify for their second year, we're getting more regional days out of them," he says.
We're standing by for a Tony Burke press conference
We're expecting him to announce changes to the backpacker visa rules.

After pushback from the farming, tourism and hospitality sectors, the government is expected to delay a proposed ballot system for backpackers seeking second- and third-year visas until early next year, avoiding disruption to the summer seasonal workforce.
The cap on third-year visas could also rise from the originally proposed 5,000 figure, alongside longer regional work requirements.

Chalmers says 'substantial' spending cuts are coming
In a speech to the ASIC Forum, Treasurer Jim Chalmers says cuts will be the "main focus" of December's mid-year budget update, but that there is a "fine balance" to strike.
"It will cut enough, but not too much," he says.
"We take seriously and embrace our responsibilities in the fight against inflation."
Still no details on whether this will be a net save, where the total savings are greater than any new spending. Chalmers says he and "the colleagues" are still putting the finishing touches on.
No word also on what they will be, although Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said this month the public service would be one focus for some "belt tightening".
Key Event
Spender's CGT alternative 'not the right model': Chalmers
Jim Chalmers isn't considering adopting an alternative model to the capital gains tax discount as proposed by independent Allegra Spender.
Spender's model would replace the government's planned inflation-based deduction in favour of a 40 per cent CGT discount on productive assets.
The Greens on Monday flagged they were open to considering the Spender model. Chalmers told reporters in Sydney he sought Treasury advice on plan after a long discussion with Spender about it.
"I have a lot of respect for Allegra and the contribution that she makes but there are important reasons why I don't think the model that she's put forward is the right model," he says.
Chalmers says he put the advice of Treasury to Spender in a letter that he says will be released in coming days.

"To summarise those reasons, the proposal that Allegra has put forward in the view of the Treasury, is unlikely to be simpler, unlikely to be fairer, unlikely to lead to a more productive economy. In fact, in their view, in its view, it's more likely to be more complex," he says.
Key Event
Chalmers declares he'll still be treasurer at next election
Jim Chalmers is rejecting a suggestion his colleagues have lost faith in him and insists he'll still be treasurer come the next election.
The treasurer has been under pressure in recent weeks. Some within caucus have vented frustrations about the government's tax changes. Other unnamed sources suggested Chalmers should be replaced.
Asked if he was a liability to Labor's re-election chances, Chalmers responds he doesn't "spend a lot of time dwelling" on the politics or commentary.
"I understand when you're embarking on big ambitious reform, particularly economic reform, especially tax reform, none of that is easy," says.
"I knew that going in."I'll leave the commentary on me, or on the internal politics, to others."
"I knew that going in.
"I'll leave the commentary on me, or on the internal politics, to others."
Chalmers says the feedback about him is an "inevitable consequences of a treasurer pushing difficult reforms through the parliament".
The problem with British backpackers
We're expecting to hear from Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke this morning as the government softens its planned backpacker visa changes.
But these changes are unlikely to impact British backpackers, who are exempt from regional work requirements under the Australia-UK free trade agreement.
Their numbers have surged in recent years, complicating the government's efforts to reduce migration while maintaining regional workforces.

While Anthony Albanese has previously ruled out changing the UK arrangements, he hinted at a rethink ahead of meetings with his British counterpart in the Caribbean, saying backpackers should experience more than just Bondi and Coogee — a nod to possible regional work requirements.
It's a complicated diplomatic balancing act because backpacker rights are enshrined in the free trade agreement. It seems unlikely we will have a definitive answer today.
Key Event
Backpacker rules expected to change
The ABC understands changes to backpacker visa rules are imminent, with Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke due to front the media this morning.
But none of those changes would affect British backpackers, who remain exempt from regional work rules under the Australia-UK free trade agreement.
With UK arrivals surging since 2023, that exemption remains the elephant in the room for a government trying to reduce overall numbers.
More on that shortly.
McLachlan again breaks ranks on EU free trade deal
Andrew McLachlan has already broken ranks with the Coalition on several issues this morning ... so what's another one!

The Liberal senator isn't too happy with the opposition's position on the Australia-EU free trade agreement. As it stands, the Coalition opposes the deal amid concerns it would bind Australia to climate targets.
McLachlan reiterates that he's willing to cross the floor to support the deal as he urged colleagues to put "partisan politics aside".

"I do appreciate there are some sectors that don't feel they are advanced sufficiently, but it is a negotiation with another trading bloc. And I think that you shouldn't punish those that are going to do very well by those who didn't do as much as they expected. It's just I don't think it's a liberal principle, collective punishment."
McLachlan says there are "many liked-minded individuals" in the party room. But he concedes he could be criticised for being "too outspoken".
McLachlan pans 'illogical' Coalition plan to gut climate funding
Andrew McLachlan says he is "totally opposed" to a Coalition plan to slash climate funding as part of a bid to save the budget bottom line $31b.
The Liberal senator criticised the plan as "gutting" for the sake of it.

"It might be saving in the sense of a financial saving but at what cost to the environment? I found a great difficulty with the approach because you're taking away for example, the Climate Change Authority, which is telling you what you need to do to achieve your targets under Paris – of which we are still committed to," he tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast.
"I thought it was illogical".
"I thought it was illogical".
McLachlan, who voted for Sussan Ley in the Liberal leadership spill back in February, is asked if he thinks Angus Taylor is doing a better job.
He repeats that he doesn't think Ley got a fair chance. But the Coalition was getting "some gains" and he wished his leaders well.
Key Event
Lib senator lashes his own side over 'petty' COP criticism
A Liberal senator has criticised his own side for making "petty" criticisms about Australia's involvement at a UN climate conference instead of focusing on policy.
The Coalition has criticised the cost of the government's engagement at COP31, including the $32,000 spent to run a coffee cart at Australia's pavilion.
Andrew McLachlan says the opposition should be focused on the environment rather than making criticisms just because "it makes the papers".

"I think the criticisms from my own side of politics are petty. We are a long way from many parts of the world. This is an opportunity to gather and be on the national stage. And I'm proud of the fact that we are heavily engaged in COP," he tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast.
"Well, I think a focus on coffee rather than climate targets and how we're going to cooperate in the world to save our planet. I would rather discuss that than how many coffees we've served."
Ayres says it's in Australia's interest to sign up to US-led AI supply chain agreement
Australia has joined a US-led agreement to protect the sensitive technology and supply chains needed to develop advanced artificial intelligence.
The agreement aims to reduce a reliance on nations that could disrupt access to critical minerals.

Industry Minister Tim Ayres says it's part of the "web of trade and supply chain agreements" signed by the government in recent years. He pointed to the EU-Australia Free Trade Agreement and deals around critical minerals to make his point.

"It's in our interest to participate in those supply chains and and its interest to be able to access these technologies right up the value chain through to the high-end artificial intelligence capabilities as well."
Bowen releases first draft of COP deal
Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen has unveiled the first draft of a climate deal, as part of his role as president of negotiations at the UN COP climate summit in Türkiye.
Bowen says the draft contains clauses that have already been rejected by some nations, and has cautioned that the inclusion of some elements does not mean they will make the final text.

"Frankly, if we only talk about what we all agree on, if we only put in things in the broader statement that got everyone's support at this point, so early in the process, it'll be a pretty short document," he told reporters overnight.
"We need to move the dial. Which means having a conversation on things where parties currently don't quite see eye-to-eye, to help bring them closer to agreement in coming days."
The draft calls for an "accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels", including an "immediate" transition away from fossil fuels.
Charlton denies aged care home support 'rip-off' refunds given as result of media reports
Andrew Charlton has denied refunds were only offered for overcharged aged care home support service because of media reporting.

The Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission has ordered providers to refund more than $300,000 to older people on the Support at Home program amid complaints participants were being overcharged for supports such as cleaning, meal preparation and allied health.
Speaking with Seven, Charlton described some of the costs as "rip-offs".

"Some of these are rip-offs and they're rip-offs on older Australians and they rip-offs on taxpayers. That's why the government has stepped in here to make sure that we give the regulator … powers to compel transparency and to take action," he says."That action can include refunds and that's what you've seen in this case."

"Some of these are rip-offs and they're rip-offs on older Australians and they rip-offs on taxpayers. That's why the government has stepped in here to make sure that we give the regulator … powers to compel transparency and to take action," he says.
"That action can include refunds and that's what you've seen in this case."
Charlton rejected a suggestion the refunds only came after the media reported on it.
"More than 40 organisations have been reviewed for their pricing, and some of the actions you've seen today are the result of some of those investigations," he says.
Key Event
Support at Home providers forced to refund more than $300,000

Aged care providers have been forced to refund more than $300,000 for overcharging participants on the Support at Home aged care scheme, according to new figures from the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission.
Since the Support at Home scheme began in November last year, participants have complained about being overcharged for the supports they receive, such as cleaning, meal preparation and allied health.

Health and Ageing Minister Mark Butler yesterday said it was "pretty shocking" to see some participants being "ripped off" and called on the commission to do its job and "take action" against bad providers.
The commission says it is securing refunds and any "providers charging unreasonable or unjustifiable prices can expect scrutiny".

"We will require non-compliance to be addressed, including refunds or credits where appropriate, and may escalate to formal enforcement action if a provider fails to act," the commission said in a statement.
Australia and Philippines agree to consult on security threats
Australia and the Philippines have agreed to consult each other if either country faces a threat to its sovereignty or security.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese met Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr in Manila on Monday night, where the pair agreed to strengthen their defence ties.

The new agreement means the countries will consult each other if a situation arises that threatens their sovereignty or shared security interests, although it doesn't commit either country to coming to the other's defence.
It comes after the two nations signed a separate deal to expand military cooperation.
The leaders also discussed security at sea, boosting trade and investment, and Australia's efforts to keep children safe online, including its under-16 social media ban.
Albanese presses Laos PM over deaths of Australian teenagers
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has pressed his Laotian counterpart for answers over the deaths of two Australian teenagers from suspected methanol poisoning almost two years ago.
Bianca Jones and Holly Bowles, both aged 19, were among six tourists who died after consuming suspected methanol-laced alcohol in the tourist town of Vang Vieng.

A distillery owner faced lesser charges relating to the production of harmful alcohol and operating an illegal business earlier this year, but authorities have said there is insufficient evidence to link anyone to the deaths.

Albanese raised the case directly with Laos's new Prime Minister Saleumxay Kommasith during a meeting in Manila on Monday night, acknowledging the families' concerns about the seriousness of the charges.
"We want, I think, a speedy resolution, if that's at all possible," Albanese said.
Saleumxay insists his government is doing everything it can to bring those responsible to justice but has acknowledged the process had dragged on.
He says authorities are still gathering evidence, including from Thailand, and investigating both alcohol producers and others potentially involved.
Key Event
Another headache for Labor as Greens weigh up CGT alternative
Months after handing down the budget the government is once again facing possible delays to its tax reforms.
The Greens are entertaining the idea of backing a plan by independent MP Allegra Spender to overhaul Labor's capital gains tax discount changes.
Under Labor's CGT tweak, the originally 50 per cent discount is mostly gone and instead replaced by an inflation-based deduction. A minimum tax rate of 30 per cent also applies to capital gains.
But Spender wants to replace that with a 40 per cent CGT discount on productive assets, which means the inflation-based deduction would largely apply only to housing.
The ABC understands the government is unwilling to take up the idea.
The Greens, who have the balance of power in the Senate, say they're willing to look a Spender's proposal describing it as "very interesting".
It leaves the government with more potential headaches as it tries to get its legislative agenda wrapped up before the end of the year.
